questions.text: In 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to grant women the right to vote. Which of the following was the MOST important leader of the NZ women's suffrage movement, and what was the key tactic she used?
options: Helen Clark — she led marches in Wellington in the 1890s
Kate Sheppard — she organised a series of mass petitions to Parliament; the 1893 petition contained nearly 32,000 signatures (about a quarter of all adult European women in NZ at the time)
Whina Cooper — she led the 1893 Land March from Te Hāpua to Parliament
Jacinda Ardern — she introduced women's suffrage as Prime Minister
questions.expectedAnswer: Kate Sheppard — she organised a series of mass petitions to Parliament; the 1893 petition contained nearly 32,000 signatures (about a quarter of all adult European women in NZ at the time)
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is Kate Sheppard with the petition tactic.

Here's why:
Kate Sheppard led the suffrage movement in NZ throughout the 1880s–90s, organising successive petitions to Parliament. The 1893 petition was the largest in NZ history at the time.
Her image is on the NZ $10 note.
Helen Clark and Jacinda Ardern were Prime Ministers who came much later. Whina Cooper was a major Māori leader famous for the 1975 Land March, NOT the 1893 land march (a common trap).
Exam tip: knowing the TACTIC used (petition) lifts a recall question to a merit-level explanation.

questions.text: The New Zealand Wars (Land Wars) of the 1840s–1870s were primarily fought over land, sovereignty and authority. Which choice CORRECTLY identifies the MAIN sides AND a major long-term consequence?
options: New Zealand vs Australia; the consequence was a free-trade agreement

The British Crown and colonial settlers vs Māori iwi; the consequence was large-scale land confiscation under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, including over 1.2 million acres taken from Waikato iwi
North Island Māori vs South Island Māori; the consequence was a single Māori nation
New Zealand vs France; the consequence was the loss of French colonies in the Pacific
questions.expectedAnswer: The British Crown and colonial settlers vs Māori iwi; the consequence was large-scale land confiscation under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, including over 1.2 million acres taken from Waikato iwi
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the British Crown vs iwi option WITH the raupatu consequence.

Here's why:
The New Zealand Wars were a series of conflicts (Northern War, Waikato War, Taranaki Wars) fought between the British Crown and various iwi, primarily over land and sovereignty.
A major long-term consequence was the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, which allowed huge land confiscations (raupatu) — particularly affecting Waikato-Tainui, who lost about 1.2 million acres.
Raupatu lies behind many modern Treaty settlements, including Waikato-Tainui's settlement in 1995.
Exam tip: knowing both the cause AND a long-term consequence is what merit-level history requires.

questions.text:
Explain ONE significant long-term IMPACT of the New Zealand Wars (Land Wars) on Māori communities. Your answer must:
• name a specific impact
• give a SPECIFIC historical example (named iwi, place, or piece of legislation)
• explain how this impact is still felt today.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for the impact + a specific historical example.

1 mark for explaining how the impact is still felt today.

Examples of strong answers:

Land confiscation (raupatu) — after the Waikato War the Crown confiscated approximately 1.2 million acres of Waikato land under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863. This devastated Waikato-Tainui economically and socially. Still felt today: the 1995 Waikato-Tainui Treaty settlement was a direct response, but the loss of ancestral land cannot be fully restored, and Waikato-Tainui still works to recover and protect remaining sites.

Loss of economic base — after losing their land, many Taranaki Māori had no farming or fishing base and became landless labourers. Still felt today: the long-running Taranaki settlements process and Crown apologies show the wars' lasting effect on iwi prosperity.

Kīngitanga movement — the wars were part of why the Māori King Movement was established, to unite tribes and resist further land sales. Still felt today: the Kīngitanga continues, with the King/Queen at Tūrangawaewae Marae playing an important role in modern NZ public life.

Long-term grievances and the Waitangi Tribunal — many of the claims investigated by the Waitangi Tribunal today relate directly to the Land Wars era.

Do not award the second mark unless the answer clearly links to the present day.

questions.text: The New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 protects rights and freedoms in NZ. Which option correctly identifies a right protected by the Act AND a right that is NOT?
options: Protected: free unlimited internet for all. NOT protected: freedom of expression
Protected: freedom of expression and the right to a fair trial. NOT protected: a right to free university education
Protected: a guaranteed job. NOT protected: freedom of religion
Protected: the right to own a sports car. NOT protected: freedom of peaceful assembly
questions.expectedAnswer: Protected: freedom of expression and the right to a fair trial. NOT protected: a right to free university education
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the freedom of expression / no free university option.

Here's why:
The NZ Bill of Rights Act 1990 affirms civil and political rights — including freedom of expression (s14), freedom of religion (s13), peaceful assembly (s16), the right to vote (s12), and the right to a fair trial.
It does NOT cover economic or social entitlements like free internet, free university, guaranteed jobs or the right to own particular goods.
Exam tip: civil and political rights = NZBORA; social and economic rights are covered by separate laws and policies.

questions.text:
The chart above shows NZ's population by ethnicity from the 2023 Census (people could identify with more than one group, so totals exceed 100%).

A town in NZ has 12,500 residents and the same ethnic proportions as the national figures.

(a) Calculate approximately how many residents would identify as Māori.
(b) Calculate approximately how many residents would identify with BOTH NZ European AND Māori, IF half of those who identify as Māori in this town also identify as NZ European. Show your working for BOTH parts.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: 17% of 12,500 = 0.17 × 12,500 = 2,125 residents identify as Māori (part a).

Step 2: Half of those also identify as NZ European = 2,125 ÷ 2 ≈ 1,063 (part b).

Step 3: The expected answer for part (b) is 1,063 (rounded). Accept 1062–1063 if working is shown.

Step 4: Both calculations must be visible in working for the mark.

Note: in the 2023 Census people could identify with more than one ethnicity, so totals exceed 100%.

questions.text:
Explain TWO different ways that Pasifika cultures CONTRIBUTE to New Zealand society. For EACH way you must:
• name the contribution
• give a specific NZ example
• explain the broader impact on NZ society.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark per contribution IF the answer includes name + specific example + broader impact. 2 required.

Examples of strong answers:

Arts and performance — Pasifika music, dance and visual arts are celebrated through events like the Pasifika Festival in Auckland (one of the largest Pacific Island cultural festivals in the world, attracting tens of thousands of visitors). Broader impact: this enriches NZ's identity as a Pacific nation and supports tourism and the creative economy.

Sport — A high proportion of All Blacks, Black Ferns, Silver Ferns and NRL players are of Pacific descent. Broader impact: this strengthens NZ's international sporting reputation and provides role models for Pacific youth.

Language — Samoan is the third most spoken language in NZ; Tongan, Cook Islands Māori, Niuean and Fijian are also widely spoken. Pacific Language Weeks are celebrated nationally. Broader impact: this maintains linguistic diversity and supports identity for Pacific young people.

Workforce — Pacific peoples are strongly represented in healthcare, education, construction and the primary sector. Broader impact: Pacific workers fill essential roles, especially in the Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme that supports horticulture in regions like Hawke's Bay.

Education — Polyfest (the ASB Polyfest in Auckland) is the largest Māori and Pacific secondary schools cultural festival in the world. Broader impact: it strengthens cultural pride and gives young people a stage to lead.

Do not award the second mark for one-line answers without examples.

questions.text: All people in NZ have responsibilities as well as rights. Which of the following is BOTH a legal responsibility AND a civic responsibility for adult New Zealanders?
options: Serving in the military — it is compulsory in NZ
Obeying the law (legal) AND, if called, serving on a jury (a civic duty)
Attending church every Sunday
Speaking English at all times in public spaces
questions.expectedAnswer: Obeying the law (legal) AND, if called, serving on a jury (a civic duty)
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is obeying the law + serving on a jury.

Here's why:
Obeying the law applies to everyone in NZ, citizens and residents alike — it's a legal responsibility.
Serving on a jury (when summoned) is a civic responsibility for citizens — it is required by law and helps the justice system function.
NZ does NOT have compulsory military service (it was abolished after WWII), there is no requirement to attend church (NZ has freedom of religion), and there is no requirement to speak English (NZ has three official languages: English, Te Reo Māori and NZ Sign Language).
Exam tip: distinguish between things you MUST do (obey laws, pay taxes) and things you SHOULD do (vote, volunteer).

questions.text: Climate change is having significant effects on Pacific Island nations. Explain ONE specific way climate change is affecting Pacific Island communities AND ONE specific reason why this is relevant to New Zealand. Use a SPECIFIC example or named country in your answer.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for a specific impact on Pacific Island communities (must include a named country or specific example).

1 mark for a specific reason this matters to NZ.

Impacts on Pacific Islands (any one):

Sea level rise threatens low-lying nations such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Marshall Islands. Tuvalu is so low that some communities are already losing land and salt water is contaminating the fresh water lens that crops depend on.

More intense cyclones — Cyclone Winston devastated Fiji in 2016; Cyclone Gabrielle hit NZ and parts of the Pacific in 2023.

Ocean warming and acidification damage coral reefs, threatening fisheries that island communities depend on for food and income.

Food security — changing rainfall affects taro and breadfruit crops.

Relevance to NZ (any one):

Close family and cultural ties — many New Zealanders have Pacific heritage; Tuvalu, for example, has more people living in NZ than at home.

Climate migration — NZ's Pacific Access Category visa allows a quota of Pacific Island citizens to migrate each year.

NZ's own territories (Tokelau, Niue, Cook Islands) are directly affected by sea level rise.

NZ provides aid and works with Pacific nations through the Pacific Islands Forum.

NZ itself faces similar climate impacts (e.g. coastal erosion in Hawke's Bay, more flooding).

Do NOT award full marks if no specific named country/example is given on either side.

questions.text: The United Nations was established in 1945 after World War II. Which of the following BEST describes the UN's primary purpose AND a real way New Zealand contributes to it?
options: To control the economies of all countries; NZ contributes by setting global interest rates
To maintain international peace and security and promote cooperation among nations; NZ contributes by participating in UN peacekeeping missions and supporting the Sustainable Development Goals
To enforce English as the world's only language; NZ contributes by teaching English globally
To create one world government with one army; NZ contributes by giving up its parliament
questions.expectedAnswer: To maintain international peace and security and promote cooperation among nations; NZ contributes by participating in UN peacekeeping missions and supporting the Sustainable Development Goals
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the peace/security + peacekeeping option.

Here's why:
The UN was founded in 1945 to prevent another world war and to encourage international cooperation. Its core purposes are peace and security, human rights, and economic and social development.
NZ was a founding member, has served on the UN Security Council, and contributes troops to peacekeeping operations (e.g. in East Timor and the Middle East).
The other options are myths about the UN ('one world government', 'controls economies').
Exam tip: NZ's role in international organisations is a popular Year 10 question.

questions.text:
NZ's population has become much more diverse through immigration over the past 150 years.

In an extended response, DISCUSS the benefits AND challenges of cultural diversity in NZ. Your answer MUST:
• explain at least TWO clear BENEFITS with NZ examples
• explain at least ONE clear CHALLENGE with a NZ example
• consider at least TWO DIFFERENT PERSPECTIVES (e.g. new immigrants, tangata whenua/Māori, long-established communities, second-generation NZers) — and these perspectives must DISAGREE on something
• reach a CLEAR JUDGEMENT at the end about how NZ should manage diversity in future.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks total. Award one mark for each criterion below.

1 mark — TWO clear BENEFITS with NZ examples:
• Economic — skilled migrants in healthcare and IT (NZ has long relied on overseas-trained nurses and doctors, especially in rural areas).
• Cultural enrichment — Diwali Festival of Lights in Auckland and Wellington; Lunar New Year celebrations; growth of diverse cuisines in NZ cities.
• Population growth — immigration helps offset NZ's ageing population and skill shortages.
• International connections — diaspora communities support trade with Asia, the Pacific and beyond.

1 mark — ONE clear CHALLENGE with NZ example:
• Discrimination/racism — increased reports of racism towards Asian New Zealanders during COVID-19; Christchurch mosque attacks in 2019 showed extreme consequences of intolerance.
• Pressure on services — rapid population growth in Auckland has put pressure on housing, transport and schools.
• Integration — overseas qualifications not always recognised, leaving migrants underemployed.
• Cultural tensions — different values can lead to misunderstanding.

1 mark — TWO perspectives that DISAGREE on something. For example:
• A new migrant might want easier recognition of overseas qualifications and stronger anti-discrimination laws.
• A Māori perspective might be concerned that increasing diversity should NOT come at the cost of the Treaty partnership — Māori are not 'just another minority', they are tangata whenua and the Crown's Treaty partner.
• A long-established Pākehā community might support diversity but worry about the pace of change.
• A second-generation NZer might feel pulled between their parents' culture and NZ culture.

1 mark — Specific NZ examples + clear judgement:
• Historical context — Chinese miners on the Otago goldfields (1860s), the Chinese poll tax (1881–1944, formally apologised for in 2002), post-WWII Pacific migration, more recent migration from Asia, Africa and the Middle East.
• Specific policies — points-based skilled migrant category, Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme, refugee quota.
• Reaches a CLEAR JUDGEMENT — e.g. 'NZ should welcome diversity but uphold its Treaty obligations to Māori as tangata whenua and invest in support services so newcomers can integrate fairly.'

Do NOT award full marks for answers that list facts without considering different perspectives, or that fail to reach a judgement.
